name: Roviana
confidence_why: Corston-Oliver 2002 puts non-contrastive stress on the first syllable of disyllabic roots and on the first two syllables of longer roots, Schuelke 2020 puts it on the penult with antepenultimate stress before echo vowels, and the only other statement, Waterhouse 1928's remark that the accent usually falls on the first syllable, cannot decide between them for words of three or more syllables.

catalog_quote: [Corston-Oliver 2002 §1.3] Stress is not contrastive. Stress is assigned independently to roots and to material which precedes the root (i.e. prefixes and reduplicated material) as follows: (i) Roots of one syllable, with the exception of prepositions and articles, take stress ... (ii) Roots of two syllables are stressed on the initial syllable: /'zama/ 'talk' /'talo/ 'taro' ... (iii) Roots of more than two syllables are stressed on the first and second syllables: /'e'hara/ 'blood' /'zi'para/ 'red' /'ga'loto/ 'struggle' /'si'gareti/ 'cigarette' /'ba'sioto/ 'crocodile' ... All material which precedes the root (prefixes and reduplicated material) is assigned stress as if it were a single root. ... The transitive suffix /-i/ takes stress ... new_statements.quote: Roviana has a general pattern of penultimate stress; however, there are apparent exceptions which display antepenultimate stress. Generally, Roviana only displays antepenultimate stress on words which have an echo-vowel, suggesting that stress assignment is “blind” to the echo-vowel. ... (4) Penultimate stress in 2-, 3-, and 4-syllable words /‘he.na/ ‘eat’ /‘pa.tu/ ‘stone’ /‘ha.mbu/ ‘to fish’ /tu.‘mae/ ‘to understand’ /nu ‘ŋgu.ru/ ‘to enter’ /ma.ta.‘ɣu.tu/ ‘to fear’ (5) Anti-penultimate stress in 3-syllable words /‘to.mo.ko/ ‘war canoe’ /‘ɣa.ru.mu/ ‘type of crab’ /‘ko.mo.lo/ ‘to smile’ A full discussion of stress is beyond the scope of this brief sketch and should be the topic of future work.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for rovi1238 (catalog-all-2026-09-12, classification 'descriptions disagree', empty rule string) already quotes this exact passage verbatim as its second primary (the secondary-stress rule = Schuelke penult with echo-vowel antepenults). Re-reading confirms the quote, the page numbers (20-21) and the hedge. It CONTRADICTS the catalog's first primary, Corston-Oliver 2002 §1.3 (pp. 468-469): left-edge root stress, roots of 3+ syllables stressed on syllables 1 and 2 (/'si'gareti/, /'ba'sioto/), affix-conditioned; the two agree only on non-contrastiveness (implicit in Schuelke) and on initial=penult for disyllables. Nothing new beyond what the catalog holds.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (2-, 3- and 4-syllable examples given: 'he.na, tu.'mae, nu'ŋgu.ru, ma.ta.'ɣu.tu). Words ending in a paragogic echo vowel are stressed as if the echo vowel were not there, so they surface with antepenultimate stress ('to.mo.ko, 'ɣa.ru.mu, 'ko.mo.lo). Explicitly provisional: 'a general pattern', 'beyond the scope of this brief sketch'. No weight conditioning, no morphological conditioning mentioned.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; one stress mark per word, no primary/secondary distinction drawn.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress on echo-vowel-final words (stress 'blind' to the echo vowel); footnote 3 (p. 20) notes some forms only appear to have echo vowels, e.g. tomoko 'war canoe' < *toa.moko, whose historical final vowel is now indistinguishable from an added echo vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuelke 2020 describes Roviana of New Georgia (Western Province, Solomon Islands) from his own elicitation recordings (PS1-001 to PS1-006 cited in the phonology sketch); no particular dialect is named in the stress section. The 1926 phrase book was not opened, so its variety is unverified.

readall_conflicts: The only listed work opened (Schuelke 2020) is already one of the catalog's two conflicting primaries, so the standing conflict is unchanged: Schuelke 2020 (pp. 20-21) gives right-edge penultimate stress on 2-4-syllable words (/nu'ŋgu.ru/, /ma.ta.'ɣu.tu/) with antepenult on echo-vowel words, hedged as provisional; Corston-Oliver 2002 (§1.3, pp. 468-469, held by the project from the earlier reading) gives non-contrastive left-edge root stress with 3+-syllable roots stressed on syllables 1 and 2 (/'e'hara/, /'si'gareti/) and affix-specific behaviour. The accounts coincide for disyllables (initial = penult) and Corston-Oliver's double marking on trisyllables spans both of Schuelke's variants, but 4-syllable forms conflict outright (/'si'gareti/ vs /ma.ta.'ɣu.tu/). A third voice already in this folder, Waterhouse 1928 dictionary preface p. ix ('the accent in the great majority of cases falls on the first syllable'), sides with the left-edge/initial account. Waterhouse 1926 (phrase book), which might add a fourth, could not be downloaded (PuRe 403).

audit.recode_to: Resolve 'descriptions disagree' in favour of Corston-Oliver 2002 (the record's own stated fallback: set by morphology / left-edge root-initial, non-contrastive), keeping Schuelke 2020's penult note as a flagged provisional dissent; add Waterhouse 1928 p. ix as third primary.
audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are verbatim in copies we hold at the stated locators; the 2002 passage was additionally checked against a clean page scan (print p. 469), which also shows that Corston-Oliver marks syllables 1 and 2 of long roots with identical primary marks, so no ranking can be read into it. (2) The classification rests on the best descriptions that exist: a 2002 handbook sketch with a real stress section and a 2020 syntax dissertation with a self-declared provisional stress paragraph; Glottolog has no grammar/phonology above sketch level and Crossref shows no phonology or instrumental study. (3) Opening the remaining Glottolog items: Corston 1996, Ray 1926 and Todd 2000 are silent; Waterhouse 1928 (PARADISEC images, downloaded) states 'the accent in the great majority of cases falls on the first syllable', an independent third primary that agrees with Corston-Oliver's left-edge account
audit.second_reader_evidence: QUOTES (re-opened, all verbatim): (1) Corston-Oliver 2002 sec. 1.3: held the scanned textcarries every sentence of the catalog quote, header 'ROVIANA 469' falls after the first two sentences so pp. 468-469 is right; the downloaded clean page render (printed p. 469) shows /'e'hara/, /'zi'ŋara/ (scanned 'zi'para'), /'ga'loto/, /'si'gareti/, /'ba'sioto/ with two identical raised primary marks, so the compilers is right that no primary/secondary ranking is recoverable from print. (2) Schuelke 2020: held schuelke2020_
